headline: July inflation landed exactly on forecast, the odds of a September rate rise fell to 38% from roughly half, and the bond market unwound the hedge it had built — with producer prices and jobless claims due at 8:30 this morning.
stance: The event everyone waited on passed without a surprise. July consumer prices rose 0.1% on the month and 3.4% over the past year, down from 3.5% in June, with the core measure that strips out food and energy up 0.2% on the month and 2.5% on the year — every one of those figures exactly what forecasters had penciled in. Interest-rate futures moved on it anyway: the chance the Fed leaves its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in September rose to 62% by late Wednesday morning from 52% a day earlier, which puts a quarter-point rise at 38%, down from roughly half going into the print. Stocks took the relief: the S&P 500 rose 0.26% to 7,748.50 and the Nasdaq 100 0.54% to 26,588.49, while the Dow slipped 0.04% to 53,770.27. The clearest tell was in the hedging. The MOVE index — the Treasury market's version of the VIX — fell to 72.1 from 77.9, wiping out two sessions of build-up in one day, and the VIX fell to 14.55 from 15.28. The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.68% from 4.70%. What is left is the other half of the price picture: producer prices and weekly jobless claims arrive at 8:30am ET, and factory-gate costs are where oil near $90 would show up first.

news.head: Inflation came in exactly as forecast
news.body: The government's July consumer-price report, released Wednesday at 8:30am ET, showed prices up 0.1% on the month after falling 0.4% in June, and up 3.4% over the past year from 3.5% in June. The core measure that excludes food and energy rose 0.2% on the month, after being unchanged in June, and 2.5% over the year. Forecasters had looked for 0.1% and 3.4% on the headline and 0.2% and 2.5% on core — a rare print that matched on all four.

news.head: September moved even though the number didn't surprise
news.body: Interest-rate futures pricing put the chance the Fed holds its target range at 3.50%-3.75% in September at 62% late Wednesday morning, up from 52% a day earlier; the implied odds of a quarter-point rise fell to 38% from roughly half. An in-line reading was enough because it left last week's jobs contraction as the loudest recent data point rather than overriding it. One more inflation report lands before the September 15-16 meeting.

news.head: The fuel line is the part with a tail
news.body: Energy prices fell 1.5% in July and gasoline fell 2.9%, which is what held the headline to 0.1%. Measured against a year ago, though, energy is up 14.7% and gasoline 24.6% — the war-driven move is in the annual figures and has not yet worked through the rest of the basket. Shelter rose just 0.1% on the month and 3.2% over the year, food 0.1% and 3.0%, and services excluding energy 0.2% and 3.0%.

news.head: Cisco beat and raised, with $9.3 billion of AI orders for the year
news.body: The networking company reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $17.3 billion, up 18% on a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of $1.22 a share against about $1.17 expected. It took $4 billion of AI-related orders from the largest cloud operators in the quarter, $9.3 billion for the full fiscal year. It guided the current quarter to $18.0-18.2 billion of revenue and $1.32-1.34 a share, and the full year to $72.2-73.4 billion and $5.05-5.11. The shares closed Wednesday at $123.88 ahead of the release.

news.head: The AI complex did the day's heavy lifting
news.body: CoreWeave rose 19% and Super Micro Computer 19% on Wednesday, Lumentum 14% and Nvidia 3% — the follow-through from Tuesday night's results and spending raise. Away from that, Wendy's gained on takeover news and Home Depot fell after disclosing a medical leave for its chief executive. That concentration is why the Dow finished slightly lower while the other two indices rose.

news.head: Wednesday's insider filings were small but numerous
news.body: Filings dated Wednesday show about $1.8 million bought at COE across ten separate filings by two insiders, roughly $800,000 at ACDC across four filings by two buyers, and about $542,000 at GLIBK across three filings by one buyer. The largest dollar figure still sitting in the current run of filings is roughly $10.1 million at LOCL from a single buyer, dated Monday.

implications: An in-line print sets the lean, it does not settle the decision. Hold odds at 62% mean the market now treats a September pause as the base case rather than a coin flip, but with one more inflation report and a retail-sales figure due Friday before the meeting, this is a lean built on two data points, not a conclusion.

The repricing was of policy, not of inflation itself. The 10-year breakeven — the annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next decade — eased only to 2.26% from 2.27%, the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield to 2.42% from 2.43%, and the gap between 2- and 10-year yields held at 48 basis points. Nothing in those three says the bond market changed its long-run view; what changed is what it expects the Fed to do in five weeks.

Producer prices this morning are the first read on whether oil is leaking into costs. Forecasters looking at today's report expect 0.1% on the month on the headline and 0.3% on the core, with the annual rates falling to about 4.8% and 4.2% from 5.5% and 4.7% — and they note prices looked subdued at the time the data was collected. Brent settled at $88.37 Wednesday from $88.95 Tuesday, so the sharpest part of the energy move sits after the survey window, not inside it.

Protection got cheaper on the news, which cuts both ways. The VIX fell to 14.55 from 15.28 and its Nasdaq counterpart to 20.97 from 22.38, yet the skew index — what investors pay for insurance against a large drop specifically — edged up to 136.5 from 135.6. Ordinary hedges were sold off after the event passed while tail hedges were not, into a market whose cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio sits at 42.3.

watch.head: Producer prices, 8:30am ET
watch.body: Forecasts centre on 0.1% for the month on the headline and 0.3% on the core measure, against June readings of -0.3% and 0.2%; on an annual basis the headline is seen easing to roughly 4.8% from 5.5% and core to 4.2% from 4.7%. Producer prices lead consumer prices, so this is where fuel and freight costs show up before they reach a shelf.

watch.head: Weekly jobless claims, 8:30am ET
watch.body: The last reading was 199,000. After July payrolls contracted by 23,000, claims are the highest-frequency check on whether the job market is genuinely deteriorating or simply cooling — and it is the labour side, not the inflation side, that has done the most to move September pricing this month.

watch.head: Applied Materials after today's close
watch.body: The chip-equipment maker reports fiscal third-quarter results, with analysts looking for about $3.39 a share on roughly $9 billion of revenue, which would be about 23% growth on a year earlier. Coming a day after Cisco named $9.3 billion of AI orders, it is the same build-out question one step further up the supply chain, at the machines that make the chips.

watch.head: Whether oil stays off the boil
watch.body: Brent settled at $88.37 Wednesday from $88.95 Tuesday and US crude at $82.58 from $83.23. Ten vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Monday against roughly 130 a day before the war, and Iran has tied any reopening to sanctions relief. With the annual energy figure at 14.7%, the crude price is the single input that could still turn a benign inflation path.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since yesterday morning: the inflation report is behind us, and it changed the odds without changing the numbers. Prices rose 0.1% on the month and 3.4% over the past year, from 3.5% in June, with core at 0.2% and 2.5% — matching forecasts on all four. Interest-rate futures pricing now puts a September hold at 62%, up from 52% a day earlier, and a quarter-point rise at 38%, down from roughly half going into the print.

Underneath the headline, the composition was benign but not settled. Energy fell 1.5% on the month and gasoline 2.9%, which is what kept the top-line figure at 0.1%; against a year earlier those same two are up 14.7% and 24.6%. Shelter rose 0.1% on the month and 3.2% over the year, food 0.1% and 3.0%, and services excluding energy 0.2% and 3.0%. All-items prices had fallen 0.4% in June, so July's small rise is a step up from a soft base.

Treasuries barely moved on the number itself: the 10-year yield closed Wednesday at 4.68% from 4.70% Tuesday, the 2-year at 4.20% from 4.22%, with the gap between them unchanged at +48 basis points. The 10-year breakeven — the annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next ten years — eased to 2.26% from 2.27% and the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield to 2.42% from 2.43%.

The hedge came off hard. The MOVE index, which measures expected swings in Treasury prices, fell to 72.1 from 77.9 — more than reversing the two-session build-up into the print, since it stood at 75.5 on Monday. That unwind, rather than the yield move, is what the bond market actually did on Wednesday.

Elsewhere in the prior close: gold rose to $4,469 from $4,427.80 and silver to $65.53 from $64.86, while Brent settled at $88.37 from $88.95 and US crude at $82.58 from $83.23. The dollar index sat at 99.99 from 99.82 and the yen at ¥159.39 from ¥159.24, still at the weak end of its three-year range. Corn was the odd mover, jumping 46 percentile points in five sessions to the 93rd percentile of its three-year range at 481 cents a bushel.
Today brings producer prices and weekly jobless claims together at 8:30am ET, retail sales tomorrow, and the minutes of the July meeting on August 19.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: speculators moved to an extended long position in gold — the 87th percentile of the past three years, up 32 percentile points in a single week. That is a contrarian-bearish lean into a metal that closed Wednesday at $4,469, up from $4,427.80 Tuesday — the crowd is leaning the same way the price has been going, which is when positioning matters most.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Wednesday's close: the S&P 500 rose 0.26% to 7,748.50 and the Nasdaq 100 0.54% to 26,588.49, ending a two-session slide, while the Dow slipped 0.04% to 53,770.27. The split tells you where the buying went — into the AI complex rather than across the market.

Cisco reported after Wednesday's close: fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $17.3 billion, up 18% on a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of $1.22 a share against about $1.17 expected, with $4 billion of AI orders in the quarter and $9.3 billion for the fiscal year. It guided the current quarter to $18.0-18.2 billion and $1.32-1.34 a share, and the full year to $72.2-73.4 billion and $5.05-5.11. The shares closed at $123.88 before the release.

The day's largest moves were the AI build-out names following through on Tuesday night's results: CoreWeave up 19%, Super Micro Computer 19%, Lumentum 14% and Nvidia 3%. Home Depot fell after disclosing a medical leave for its chief executive, and Wendy's rose on takeover news.

Protection got cheaper once the event passed: the VIX closed at 14.55 from 15.28 Tuesday and its Nasdaq-100 counterpart at 20.97 from 22.38. The skew index, which measures what investors pay for insurance against a large drop specifically, edged up to 136.5 from 135.6 — the ordinary hedges were sold, the tail hedges were not.

Breadth improved on the tech side: 63% of Nasdaq-100 members closed above their 50-day trend line, up from 55% Tuesday, and 66.5% of S&P 500 members did, from 64.9%. On the slower 200-day measure it is 72% and 70.9% respectively, both a touch lower than Tuesday — participation broadened over days, not over months.
Applied Materials reports after today's close, with analysts looking for about $3.39 a share on roughly $9 billion of revenue.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: bullish bets in Nasdaq 100 futures fell 20 percentile points on the week to the 1st percentile of the past three years, with hedgers at the opposite extreme — an extended short built the week before the index closed higher on Wednesday. Read it as scepticism rather than exuberance underneath a tape near its highs; it is fuel if the market keeps rising, not a warning that it will not.

single_name.note: (Harley-Davidson, the motorcycle maker) — an insider purchase was filed Tuesday, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and both the scan's dark-pool and options signals are live. The short position against it runs to 5.7 days of average trading volume, so it would take nearly six normal sessions of buying to unwind — which magnifies a move in either direction.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit gave back a fraction in the latest available data, which runs a day behind: the extra yield high-yield bonds pay over investment-grade was 272 basis points in Tuesday's reading, from 270 on Monday, with investment-grade spreads at 79 basis points from 78. That is noise against an oil price near $90 and an inflation print — credit is not pricing either as a problem.

The system's spare-cash cushion shrank again: the Fed's overnight reverse-repo facility held $0.7 billion Wednesday, against $1.2 billion Tuesday, with bank reserves of $2,993.3 billion and $907.3 billion in the Treasury's cash account in last Wednesday's weekly snapshot. The buffer that once absorbed trillions is now effectively a rounding error.

Short-term funding stayed quiet: the key bank-funding spreads sat at 1 basis point and the commercial-paper funding spread at 21 basis points in the latest readings, with no sign of strain in the plumbing.

Broad financial conditions remain easier than average on both national measures — one at -0.58 and the other at -0.77 in last Friday's readings, where negative means looser than normal. Stocks and credit are also moving together more than usual, with the correlation between them at 0.67.
sections.positioning: Nothing is stretched in credit, and that is the point: no positioning extreme is flagged anywhere in the credit book for a second week, with primary-dealer high-yield inventory mid-range at the 35th percentile of its three-year span. When equity and rate positioning both sit at three-year extremes, a flat credit book is the outlier worth noticing.
